title: Growth in *every* postcode?
gist: Resolution Foundation benchmarks the UK government's 'growth in every postcode' pledge against the last Parliament, where only 53 per cent of the 121 UK postcode areas saw positive living-standards growth, and flags trade and energy costs as the glaring omissions from Chancellor John Healey's investment/innovation/jobs growth strategy. Supporting research argues UK fuel retailers did not price-gouge after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, that quality-adjustment errors have massively understated historic US real consumption growth, and that cutting disability benefits is unpopular across every voting bloc including Reform.

insights.claim: Only 53 per cent of the UK's 121 high-level postcode areas recorded positive average annual living-standards growth during the last Parliament, making a pledge of growth in 100 per cent of postcodes a large step up from an already historically weak baseline.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete, trackable scoreboard for UK regional policy: the postcode-share metric becomes a measurable pass/fail on fiscal devolution and levelling-up spending that investors can monitor against government rhetoric.
insights.quote: The last Parliament achieved growth in 53 per cent of postcodes, so 100 per cent would be a considerable step up.

insights.claim: Aberdeen saw incomes fall by an average of 1.24 per cent a year in the last Parliament even while Scotland as a whole grew 0.28 per cent, marking the oil city as a structural regional loser rather than a victim of national conditions.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A named local economy in outright income decline is a candidate for targeted transition funding and a warning sign for North Sea-exposed regional assets, employers and property.
insights.quote: Bad news for Aberdeen, where income fell by an average of 1.24 per cent a year – despite Scotland seeing growth of 0.28 per cent

insights.claim: Northern Ireland posted the highest average living-standards growth of any UK region at 1.28 per cent a year over the last Parliament, while Manchester scraped positive at just 0.32 per cent a year.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Contradicts the assumption that metro-mayor city-regions are the growth engines; Northern Ireland outperforming flagship English metros reframes where regional allocation and devolution credit should flow.
insights.quote: Northern Ireland experienced the highest average growth of 1.28 per cent.

insights.claim: There is no meaningful north-south divide in living-standards growth within England, and London postcodes collectively underperformed the UK average despite enormous internal variation.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Undercuts the dominant framing of UK regional policy; if the real dispersion is within London rather than between north and south, geographically-targeted investment theses based on the north-south axis are mispriced.
insights.quote: there is no big north south divide (at least within England) with the collection of many London postcodes varying hugely but falling by a touch more overall than the UK average

insights.claim: Measuring growth at the 121 two-letter postcode-area level is a deliberately generous test of the 'growth in every postcode' pledge, because finer geographic granularity would expose far more pockets of decline.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Expect the government to claim success on coarse geography; any independent scorecard using full postcodes will show a much worse hit rate, creating a gap between headline claims and reality.
insights.quote: We’ve arguably gone easy on them by using the 121 high-level postcode areas in the UK (the first two letters of your postcode).

themes.theme: Healey growth strategy: gaps and levers

insights.claim: The two biggest omissions from Chancellor John Healey's growth strategy are trade and energy costs, both described as major drags on the UK economy and both largely outside the government's immediate control.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: UK industrial energy costs and trade frictions remain unaddressed policy risks; expect continued margin pressure on energy-intensive UK manufacturers and pressure for a future EU trade reset.
insights.quote: The biggest gaps, to my mind, were trade and energy costs. Two big drags on the economy, largely beyond the government’s immediate gift
insights.locator: Healey has made his priorities clear.

insights.claim: Raising the National Wealth Fund's annual investment to £8.8 billion by 2030-31 would restore UK public investment to the level the European Investment Bank supplied before the EU referendum, and is achievable within existing fiscal rules.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified ask ahead of the Budget: a scale-up of the NWF and British Business Bank would channel multi-billion-pound flows into UK infrastructure and growth-equity, a direct tailwind for co-investors in those pipelines.
insights.quote: Increasing the NWF’s annual investment to £8.8 billion by 2030-31 would be enough to match the European Investment Bank’s pre-referendum level of investment.
insights.locator: There's scope for boosting investment further

insights.claim: HM Treasury's decision to cut the discount rate mechanically makes long-term project investment easier to justify, but only because the underlying assumption about future growth has become more pessimistic.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: An accounting change, not an economic improvement — expect more long-dated UK infrastructure projects to clear appraisal hurdles, while the same input implies weaker long-run growth and lower real yields.
insights.quote: HMT’s decision to cut the discount rate will make investment in long-term projects easier – even if it’s because we’re more pessimistic about future growth.
insights.locator: There's scope for boosting investment further

insights.claim: The UK economy has been changing shape at historically slow rates over the last twenty years, meaning the binding constraint is economic dynamism and reallocation rather than the unicorn-and-scale-up innovation agenda the Chancellor emphasised.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Policy aimed at creating tech champions will not fix stagnant productivity if capital and labour cannot move between sectors; watch for whether Budget measures touch reallocation frictions (planning, insolvency, labour mobility) rather than just startup subsidy.
insights.quote: Over the last twenty years our economy has actually been changing shape at historically slow rates. We need more dynamism as well as more innovation, but that is a much tougher political message
insights.locator: On innovation, the Chancellor focused on

insights.claim: The UK's underemployed age groups are the young and the over-50s, and participation in education is an underdiscussed driver of the NEET rate that determines future skills and living standards.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: With the aggregate employment rate already high internationally, incremental UK labour supply must come from youth and over-50s — the pressure point for training providers, education policy and employers' hiring pipelines.
insights.quote: Participation in education remains an underdiscussed factor in our NEET rate

insights.claim: Fiscal devolution is set to be the central mechanism of the government's 'growth in every postcode' agenda, per Healey's first major speech as Chancellor.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Expect devolved revenue-raising and spending powers in the Budget — a structural shift in where UK public capital is allocated and a new layer of regional fiscal counterparties.
insights.quote: As expected, fiscal devolution will be at the heart of plans for “growth in every postcode”
insights.locator: Something for the weekend | Growing pains

insights.claim: UK diesel retail margins briefly turned negative after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, meaning pump prices rose by less than retailers' input costs — the opposite of the 'greedflation' price-gouging thesis.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Evidence against margin-expansion narratives in consumer-facing energy retail; weakens the case for windfall taxes or price controls on forecourt operators and reframes retail fuel as a low-pass-through, thin-margin business during cost spikes.
insights.quote: as wholesale costs spiked, diesel margins briefly turned negative, meaning pump prices rose by less than retailers’ input costs

insights.claim: Daily searches on fuel price comparison site PetrolPrices.com jumped more than twentyfold during the 2022 cost spike, and this surge in consumer search intensity is the causal mechanism that forced retailers to restrain margins.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A reusable mechanism: in categories with cheap price-comparison infrastructure, cost shocks trigger consumer search that compresses rather than expands retail margins — screen consumer sectors by search-tool penetration when modelling inflation pass-through.
insights.quote: Daily searches on the comparison site jumped more than twentyfold as consumers hunted the best deals, forcing retailers to restrain their margins for fear of losing out.

insights.claim: The UK fuel greedflation test drew on data from 8,000 forecourts and 200 million consumer searches, giving the no-gouging finding unusually granular empirical backing.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Sample scale makes this hard for policymakers to dismiss; reduces the odds of UK fuel-sector price intervention in the next supply shock.

themes.theme: Mismeasured quality and understated real growth

insights.claim: Adjusting for unmeasured quality improvements using 5.1 million Sears catalogue product listings from 1900 to 1990 implies US real goods consumption rose 39x rather than the 10x implied by official deflators.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: If official deflators systematically overstate inflation by missing quality gains, historic real growth and productivity have been understated — a direct challenge to secular-stagnation pessimism and to how real returns are benchmarked.
insights.quote: quality change accounts for around half of the cumulative increase in prices, meaning real goods consumption rose 39x rather than the 10x implied by official deflators

insights.claim: Roughly half of the cumulative increase in US goods prices across the twentieth century was quality change rather than true inflation, implying measured inflation was substantially lower and living-standards growth substantially higher than recorded.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A mental model for today: if current statistical agencies under-adjust for quality in tech-intensive goods and AI-enhanced services, reported real growth is understated and real rates overstated.

themes.theme: Welfare politics and social media backlash

insights.claim: In 2025 only 7 per cent of Britons thought disability benefit spending should be cut while 49 per cent wanted more spending even at the cost of higher taxes, and support for cuts has never exceeded 7 per cent across four decades of British Social Attitudes data.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Welfare cuts are not a credible source of UK fiscal consolidation; Budget savings will have to come from tax or elsewhere, which raises the odds of tax rises at the next fiscal event.
insights.quote: In 2025, only 7 per cent of people thought we should spend less on disability benefits, while nearly half (49 per cent) felt we should spend more

insights.claim: Only 11 per cent of Reform voters support cutting disability benefits, showing the political obstacle to welfare reform is broad public opinion rather than Labour backbench rebellion.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Reframes UK welfare-reform risk: no realistic parliamentary majority exists for cuts regardless of which party governs, so model UK welfare spending as sticky-upward across election outcomes.
insights.quote: The truth is that spending less on disability benefits remains deeply unpopular across the political spectrum – only 11 per cent of Reform voters support cuts.

insights.claim: The regulatory and legal tide is turning against social media companies, evidenced by Australians potentially gaining the ability to switch off algorithmic feeds and Meta agreeing an £18 billion payout.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Algorithmic-feed opt-outs and multi-billion settlements are a direct threat to engagement-based ad monetisation; watch for contagion of the Australian model into other jurisdictions as a platform-sector valuation risk.
insights.quote: Recently the tide seems to turning slightly against social media companies – with the news that Australians could soon switch off their algorithms and the £18 billion payout agreed by Meta.

insights.claim: Research using over 2 million smartphone communication records finds digital communication is more harmful to mental health when it crosses income gaps, with students more depressed whether surrounded by more affluent or more deprived peers.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Identifies inequality-exposure, not screen time alone, as the harm channel — a more defensible basis for regulation and a sharper risk for platforms whose products maximise cross-strata social comparison.
insights.quote: Communicating across income gaps left students more depressed, whether they were surrounded by more affluent or more deprived peers.
